sentence: Nebraska AIM coordinator; after calling police having been choked and maced, officers instead beat and arrested him and his wife and charged them with malicious destruction of property. Released on $1,000 bail.
AIM member ('Dino') tried with Robert Robideau for the June 26, 1975 Pine Ridge shootout deaths of two FBI agents; jury accepted a self-defense argument and acquitted both in July 1976.
Young Oglala man indicted with Leonard Peltier in the June 1975 Pine Ridge FBI-agent deaths case; the charges against him were later dropped.
Wife of Nebraska AIM coordinator Bob Yellow Bird; kicked in the stomach by an arresting officer, causing her to lose her unborn child, and charged with malicious destruction of property.
AIM member (wife of Dennis Banks) cleared with the other 'Loud Hawk' defendants of the 1975 Oregon firearms/explosives charges.

Sentenced to one-to-three years for the 1973 Custer, S.D. courthouse disturbance (where a state trooper choked and beat her); confined at the South Dakota Women's Prison, Yankton from June 1, 1974 and released on parole November 15, 1974. Her son's white killer received probation.

OSCRO co-founder and Wounded Knee organizer; after surrendering and facing federal charges arising from the 1973 occupation, he was shot and killed by BIA tribal police on the Pine Ridge Reservation on October 17, 1973, in disputed circumstances.

Convicted under Michigan's felony-murder doctrine for his role in the incident in which Wayne State student Franklin Abramson was killed; sentenced to life without parole though he maintained he did not fire the fatal shot. Sentence commuted by Gov. John Engler in 1992 and released after more than two decades.

charges: Resisting arrest; inciting a riot; marijuana
convicted: Unknown — party calls charges false; marijuana charge later reduced
sentence: Coordinator of the Southern California BPP chapter, subjected through 1977 to LAPD surveillance and repeated arrests on charges the paper calls false (resisting arrest, inciting a riot, a marijuana charge later reduced).

convicted: Unknown — party says framed / self-defense; defense committee formed
sentence: Former BPP member and UC Berkeley student who spent about four months in Rikers Island jail after being charged with the murder of a bar co-manager; the paper reports he acted in self-defense and was framed.

charges: Assault and battery on a peace officer
sentence: BPP member beaten and arrested with Robert Kendrick by LAPD in April 1977 on charges the paper calls false.

BPP member known as 'Joe-Dell,' serving a 25-30 year sentence on armed-robbery charges the paper calls trumped-up when he died in custody at Central Prison, Raleigh on June 13, 1972 — ruled a heart attack but attributed by the paper to prison officials.
BPP supporter jailed for contempt (the maximum penalty) after refusing to testify in what she called the frame-up of Huey P. Newton.

Seattle BPP member arrested while selling The Black Panther and running the Free Breakfast program; charges cleared on appeal after an officer admitted arresting him to make him change his soliciting.

One of the 'High Point 4,' who ran a Free Breakfast program targeted by COINTELPRO before a 1971 police raid; released after serving more than six years of a 7-to-10-year sentence on a trumped-up assault-on-an-officer charge.

charges: Assault on a peace officer; inciting a riot
sentence: BPP member ('Sharief') beaten and arrested by LAPD in 1977 on charges the paper calls false, including assault on a peace officer and inciting a riot.
Black Marine defendant among the 'Camp Pendleton 14' charged after an alleged confrontation with a suspected KKK gathering at Camp Pendleton in 1976.
Black Marine co-defendant among the 'Camp Pendleton 14,' facing courts-martial over the 1976 confrontation with a suspected KKK meeting at Camp Pendleton.
Black Marine defendant among the 'Camp Pendleton 14,' on trial in the courts-martial arising from Black Marines' resistance to KKK activity on base in 1976.

Black Marine private given the harshest Pendleton 14 sentence — two years plus a bad-conduct discharge — at an August 1977 court-martial that drew national protest; released after five months with his sentence reduced.
Sole member of the 'Camp Pendleton 14' acquitted of charges arising from Black Marines' 1976 resistance to KKK activity at Camp Pendleton.
Charged as one of the 'Camp Pendleton 14' after Black Marines organized against KKK activity on base in 1976.
Marine sergeant among the 'Camp Pendleton 14' who pleaded guilty under pressure to charges stemming from the 1976 confrontation with a suspected KKK meeting at Camp Pendleton.
Charged over an alleged Nov. 13, 1976 confrontation with white Marines believed to be holding a KKK meeting; defendants faced up to 21–72 years while no Klan members were charged.

One of the 'Charlotte Three'; convicted in 1972 for the 1968 arson that destroyed Lazy B Stables. Received 10 years, the shortest of the three. Gov. Hunt commuted the sentences in 1979 and Parker was released.

One of the 'Charlotte Three'; convicted in 1972 for the 1968 arson at Lazy B Stables. Received the harshest sentence of the three — 25 years. After appeals failed (including to the U.S. Supreme Court), Gov. Hunt commuted the sentences in 1979 and Grant was released on parole.

Chicano organizer for Mexican people's rights in the Rio Grande Valley arrested on what the source calls false gun-smuggling charges and detained at Topo Chico prison; described as a joint U.S.–Mexican effort to entrap him.

One of the 'Dawson Five' ('Junior' Jackson) charged with the 1976 murder of a white store customer in Dawson, Georgia; an officer testified a pistol was put between his eyes during interrogation. Charges against the Dawson Five were ultimately dismissed.

One of the 'Dawson Five' charged with the 1976 murder of a white store customer in Dawson, Georgia; defendants said they were miles away drawing water at the time. Charges against the Dawson Five were ultimately dismissed.

charges: Charges arising from 1974 Atmore-Holman prison rebellion
sentence: One of the Atmore-Holman Brothers (IFA), sentenced to 15 years in what the source calls a framed prosecution over the Jan. 18, 1974 Atmore-Holman prison rebellion.

Inmates For Action (IFA) activist convicted of murdering a policeman he says he shot in self-defense during a raid on his ex-wife's home; reportedly beaten, held in a refrigerated cell and denied medical care at Atmore-Holman; appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court.
Indicted in the 1974 Atmore-Holman rebellion; 'found hanging' in the Escambia County jail before his 1975 trial. A fellow prisoner swore officials had planned his death. Deceased.
Mobile activist (also 'Casmarah Mani') and former IFA member; reportedly beaten in an attempted police lynching, then charged with robbery and held at Mt. Meigs Prison.

charges: Charges arising from 1974 Atmore-Holman prison rebellion
sentence: One of the Atmore-Holman Brothers (IFA), convicted in what the source calls a framed prosecution over the Jan. 18, 1974 Atmore-Holman prison rebellion. Name also rendered 'McGorvey' / 'Sitting Bull.'
Mobile activist (also 'Sekou Lumpen'), former IFA member and leader of the People's Community Hall; beaten by police alongside Glenn Diamond and accused of a robbery the source calls a frame-up.

charges: Charges arising from 1974 Atmore-Holman prison rebellion
sentence: One of the Atmore-Holman Brothers (IFA), convicted in what the source calls a framed prosecution over the 1974 Atmore-Holman prison rebellion. Name also spelled 'Claney.'
Named among the Atmore prisoners falsely indicted alongside Johnny Imani Harris in the killing of a guard during the 1974 Atmore-Holman prison rebellion.

charges: Charges arising from 1974 Atmore-Holman prison rebellion
sentence: One of the Atmore-Holman Brothers (IFA), sentenced to 50 years in what the source calls a framed prosecution over the 1974 Atmore-Holman prison rebellion.

Founder/leader of the Atmore-Holman prison group Inmates For Action ('Mafundi'); held in solitary confinement over 62 days for his political beliefs and targeted with frame-up marijuana and gun charges. (Earlier framed for a $34 robbery — 14 years hard labor; in 1983 convicted of rape and, as a habitual offender, sentenced to life.)
Death by electrocution; one of the Atmore-Holman Brothers, said by the Party to have no connection to the murder charge. Beaten by four guards in March 1974.

Life. Convicted with David Rice of the 1970 bombing death of an Omaha policeman on the testimony of a 15-year-old who admitted planting the bomb; one of the 'Omaha Two,' remained imprisoned for decades.
Spent seven years in Nebraska juvenile and adult institutions without ever being tried; the ACLU sued on his behalf.

convicted: Yes (second trial; first ended in hung jury)
sentence: 25 years to life. Former Black Panther and Black Liberation Army member captured Sept. 1973 and extradited to New York for the killing of two NYPD officers. Later indicted as one of the San Francisco 8; pled guilty to a lesser offense with no additional time.

charges: Escape (from Draper prison); serving a life term
sentence: Lost both legs to gangrene after being denied medical care in custody. Escaped Draper prison, recaptured in 1979, fought extradition from Oregon with ACLU help, and sued Alabama corrections officials.
Death; faced a March 10, 1978 execution date alongside Johnny Imani Harris. At Harris's request the same defense lawyers took his case.
San Quentin prisoner on trial for allegedly assaulting a guard; killed in the shootout with guards when Jonathan Jackson entered the Marin County courtroom on Aug. 7, 1970.
48 years (four consecutive 12-year terms) with no parole eligibility, imposed at age 14 after he and three friends were forced to plead guilty.

charges: Conspiracy / smuggling a gun to George Jackson (murder)
sentence: Attorney for George Jackson, accused under the prosecution's 'gun-in-a-wig' theory of smuggling a pistol to Jackson at San Quentin on Aug. 21, 1971. Surfaced after years underground and was acquitted in 1986.

convicted: Yes (jury of 11 whites and one Black)
sentence: Death (won a stay of execution). Bay Area Black man on death row who said he did not commit the murder, calling himself a victim of a local political struggle.
One of the six 'Reidsville Brothers' facing the death penalty over the July 23, 1978 Reidsville prison rebellion.
One of the six 'Reidsville Brothers' facing the death penalty over the July 23, 1978 Reidsville prison rebellion.

charges: Murder (a guard and two inmates during prison rebellion)
sentence: One of the six 'Reidsville Brothers,' charged with killing a guard and two inmates during the July 23, 1978 Reidsville rebellion and facing the death penalty; stabbed by white inmates amid alleged official collusion.

convicted: Awaiting trial (first of the six brought to trial; facing the death penalty)
sentence: One of the six 'Reidsville Brothers' facing the death penalty over the July 23, 1978 Reidsville prison rebellion; the first of the six brought to trial.
One of the six 'Reidsville Brothers,' selectively prosecuted and facing the death penalty over the July 23, 1978 Reidsville prison rebellion.

charges: Felony charge arising from an alleged traffic violation
sentence: Fulton County DA sought to imprison him and remove him from the Georgia legislature via a felony charge over an alleged traffic violation; a National Defense Committee (Ralph Abernathy, Julian Bond, Dick Gregory) formed in response.

charges: Harboring a fugitive (AIM leader Dennis Banks)
sentence: Charged with harboring Dennis Banks after 40 FBI agents armed with shotguns and M-16s surrounded his El Cerrito home; charges were later dropped.
Sentenced to 9.5–10 years for giving two marijuana cigarettes to an undercover officer; attorney Sheldon Otis called it a bust to stifle his political activities.

charges: Assault with a deadly weapon (July 1974 police raid)
sentence: Convicted with Tom Stevens and sentenced to 5½ years-to-life over the July 1974 police raid on the White Panther Party's San Francisco food-program office; a 5,000-signature petition demanded an appeal bond.

Sentenced to 5½ years-to-life for assault with a deadly weapon after firing warning shots during a July 1974 San Francisco police raid on the party's Page Street food-program office (which police then set afire); denied bail pending appeal.
The only white member of the Wilmington Ten, convicted in the trumped-up 1971 Wilmington firebombing/conspiracy case; paroled around 1977.
One of the Wilmington Ten, convicted on trumped-up firebombing/conspiracy charges from the 1971 Wilmington unrest; convictions overturned in 1980, the group pardoned in 2012.

convicted: No — Kentucky sedition statute ruled unconstitutional
sentence: Arrested with his wife Margaret on sedition charges; home raided, papers seized by Sen. John McClellan's subcommittee, house later bombed. The decade-long case reached the U.S. Supreme Court.

convicted: No — New York dropped charges for lack of evidence
sentence: One of the 'Attica Brothers' charged with kidnapping and unlawful imprisonment for allegedly taking hostages in the 1971 Attica rebellion; the state dropped the charges for lack of evidence.

convicted: Presented as a false, retaliatory prosecution; co-defendants' charges were dropped
sentence: Brother of a 17-year-old fatally shot by LAPD officers, arrested and charged with conspiring to kill the officers in what The Black Panther presented as a false, retaliatory prosecution; his friends' charges were dropped.

charges: Felony charges from clashes with police (1979 anti-Deng Xiaoping protest)
convicted: No — lived in France while case played out; ultimately resolved
sentence: Arrested during a 1979 Washington, D.C. protest against Deng Xiaoping's White House visit and faced felony charges connected to clashes with police; lived in France for a period before the matter was resolved.
institution_name: U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia

sentence: One of the 'Smyrna 7' found guilty in September 1976 of escape-related charges at the Delaware Correctional Center; the defense committee charged guard brutality, isolation and denial of an adequate defense.

charges: Charge arising from the Ronnie Horne assault (Dessie Woods case)
sentence: With Dessie Woods, was the target of an attempted rape by Ronnie Horne on June 16, 1975; charged in the case and given a suspended sentence.

A 19-year-old Black high-school student in San Francisco's Hunters Point put on trial for felony voter-registration fraud in what her attorney called a discriminatory frame-up, singled out by the DA as the first target of a 'voter fraud crackdown.'

convicted: Yes — bid for new trial denied
sentence: Black UMass-Amherst student convicted of a 1974 McDonald's robbery and sentenced to 8-12 years despite witnesses placing him on crutches at the time; his bid for a new trial was denied.
One of the 'Smyrna 7' who, per the defense committee, were forced to plead guilty to escape charges after being denied the right to present their defense.

charges: Murder of a New York police officer (during a robbery)
sentence: Black ex-serviceman arrested in 1970 and convicted of killing a New York policeman during a robbery, sentenced to 25 years to life; reported to have been beaten and identified through suggestive lineups, with a recanting witness admitting he lied; defense committee sought a new trial.

charges: Federal immigration violations (13 counts; inducing Mexican nationals to enter the U.S.)
convicted: Unknown — under federal indictment, facing up to 65 years
sentence: 13-count federal indictment carrying up to 65 years; described by supporters as a trumped-up prosecution

convicted: Yes — convicted by an all-white jury
sentence: Convicted of second-degree murder; described as a frame-up with negative forensics and discredited paid witnesses
Faced up to one year in jail; set up an appeal fund. Beaten by LAPD officers before arrest, which supporters called a racist frame-up

convicted: Yes — convicted in the 1974 Amherst robbery case
sentence: Community defense movement won a reduced 3-5 year sentence with work-release; described as a frame-up (same case as Craemen Gethers)
One of four Black protesters arrested by U.S. marshals for occupying Harris Neck land taken from Black families in 1942; released on recognizance

charges: Contempt (refusing to turn over WBAI interview tapes to prosecutors)
sentence: WBAI general radio manager jailed 30 days in 1972 for refusing to surrender tapes of phone interviews with rioting Manhattan House of Detention inmates
Life plus five years, despite no victim identifying him and no prior record; Eldson McGhee Support Committee sought his release

charges: Attempted capital murder of a police officer (5 counts)
convicted: Unknown — charged; presented as a frame-up
sentence: Grazed by a bullet and beaten by police after a car chase, then charged with five counts of attempted capital murder though he fired no shots

charges: Conspiracy; harboring an escaped federal prisoner

22-year-old Black woman condemned to North Carolina's death row along with co-defendants though only one shot was fired

convicted: Unknown — arraigned; supporters called it a frame-up
sentence: Held 2.5 years in Marion penitentiary's behavior-modification unit; taken to St. Louis in Sept. 1975 to be arraigned on charges of assaulting four guards, which supporters said was impossible for a handcuffed prisoner

convicted: Yes — first trial hung, convicted on retrial
sentence: 30-year sentence and appeal; 1972 police frame-up after organizing against alcohol sales to minors; his own attorney reportedly testified against him

convicted: Unknown — charged; presented as a frame-up
sentence: 18-year-old wounded when Houston police riddled a car with bullets, then charged with five counts of attempted capital murder despite firing no shots (gun thrown from car before the chase)

charges: Arrested in connection with the Melvin Black police-killing case (specific charges not stated)
sentence: Arrested by Oakland Police vice-squad officers inside the NAACP office in connection with the Melvin Black police-killing case

charges: Assault/shooting of police (armed clashes with Detroit STRESS unit)
sentence: Detroit youth who with two friends fought the STRESS police unit; captured after a massive manhunt and acquitted after attorney Ken Cockrel put the police on trial
Sentenced to death May 1972, then resentenced to two consecutive 220-to-440-year terms for a murder he says he did not commit
One of four Black protesters arrested at the Harris Neck land-reclamation protest; released on recognizance

convicted: No — indictments dismissed for insufficient evidence
sentence: 'Attica Brothers' rebellion leader charged over the 1971 Attica uprising; indictments dismissed for insufficient evidence

Went into hiding under an alias for three decades before being arrested.

charges: Murder of a police officer (during 1970 robbery)

sentence: Convicted of attempted murder; conviction unraveled and charges dropped after evidence showed the sergeant shot himself.

convicted: Unknown — held on the charge; found dead (hands and feet bound) in his cell on Jan. 21, 1978, ruled a suicide (disputed by the United League of Marshall County)
sentence: Died in custody Jan. 21, 1978; officials ruled suicide, United League demanded a federal probe.

convicted: Yes — convicted with Henry Dee; sentenced to death May 1972, then to two consecutive 220-to-440-year terms; supporters called it a wrongful conviction
sentence: Sentenced to death (May 1972), later to two consecutive 220-to-440-year terms.

convicted: Pretrial — Judge Bruce Wright released him without bail citing lack of record and community ties, sparking political controversy

sentence: Death sentence, later reduced to 20 years after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the death penalty for rape; SPLC attorneys pursued a new trial.
Fighting deportation to Mexico while supporting the Camp Pendleton 14.
Indicted as a Black elected official; the paper called it a framing.

charges: Charges arising from an armed confrontation (attributed to threats by white officers)

convicted: Unknown from desc — a rally demanded the charges be dropped
